newsitem.title: UK: Japan not foreign investment firms' top priority.
newsitem.headline: Japan not foreign investment firms' top priority.

text.p: European and U.S. investment banks are reassessing their ambitions in Japan after recent alliances with Japanese firms, but bankers say their focus remains elsewhere.

"U.S. firms are looking at the European market as priority number one and Japan as number two. If you are European, you probably want to acquire in the U.S. if you can," one investment banker told Reuters.
But this week's tie-up between Switzerland's SBC Warburg and the Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan (LTCB) has increased the pressure on them to decide how to approach the Japanese markets.
"It is a groundbreaking deal which has raised interest and thoughts," the banker said.

The deal comes in anticipation of Japan's "Big Bang" financial reforms, which analysts expect to shrink business in ordinary banking while boosting demand for securities and asset management services.

Foreign banks are eyeing the developments carefully, assessing what the changes imply for their business and the opportunities the reforms add to their attempts to cultivate Japan's cash-rich markets by bringing innovation and expertise.

Most are gradually building up their Tokyo presence, growing their operations organically and awaiting their chance to develop new products and expertise in a freer environment rather than acquiring Japanese firms.
And Japanese banks are casting a careful eye over possible partners, fearful they could see the most ambitious foreign players sign up with their rivals if they do not strike quickly.
By tying up with LTCB, SBC Warburg -- the investment banking arm of Swiss Bank Corp -- has stolen a march on its competitors, although not everyone is convinced the marriage will last.
"It won't work," Jordan Lewis, a management consultant specialising in strategic alliances, told Reuters on Thursday.

On Tuesday LTCB and SBC Warburg agreed to form a strategic alliance which includes three percent cross-shareholdings. Under the plan they will set up three joint firms based in Japan to cover investment banking, asset management and private banking.
Lewis said LTCB was a rigid and inward looking organisation which would not necessarily lend itself to the flexibility such a venture would require.
"I don't see those two companies dancing together very well," he added.
Others agreed implementation of the ambitious plan was likely to prove difficult, if only at the level of ironing out their cultural differences.
"If SBC and LTCB can pull it off it is going to be fantastic for them," a Tokyo banker said.
But it would not be an easy formula for others to duplicate even if they wanted to because of the difficulty of finding suitable Japanese partners.
Others have already formed less ambitious alliances, with asset-backed securitisation seen as one of the main markets to tap.

Last month British banking giant Barclays said it had agreed to begin talks on several areas of cooperation with Hokkaido Takushoku Bank Ltd, including the development of new financial products and securitisation of its assets.
But neither party has any intention of taking a stake in the other and bankers questioned how the agreement was progressing.
"There is the impression discussions may have stalled somewhat," the first investment banker said.
And in April, Bankers Trust New York Corp announced a tie-up with Nippon Credit Bank Ltd aimed at securitising real estate and other assets.
Japan is expected to end a ban next year on banks forming financial holding firms, eliminating barriers between banks, brokerages and insurers.
While existing laws require foreign firms to have different vehicles to cover these areas, it does not prevent them from attempting to achieve synergies, the Tokyo banker said.

Firms such as the recently restructured CS Group have gradually built up their Japanese presence and now have around 700 people there assigned to three business units, asset management, private banking and corporate and investment banking.
Along with many of its competitors, CS Group has said it will pursue a policy of organic growth, at least for the time being.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell (DMG), the investment banking arm of Germany's Deutsche Bank AG, has around 500 people in Japan and is also pursuing the organic growth path.

It is concentrating on its global markets business, with foreign exchange, JGB trading and debt capital markets the main supports. But as with all its competitors, it too has the goal of generating business from Japan's corporate sector in its sights.
U.S. heavyweights such as Merrill Lynch and Co Inc, the Goldman Sachs partnership and Salomon Brothers have all built up their Japanese operations, but Big Bang will bring changes for all.
Where such firms rank Japan in their priorities for expansion is open to debate, but some believe powerhouses such as Merrill could build on their retail expertise in the U.S. and adapt it to Japan.
But European players with global ambitions such as SBC Warburg, CS Group, DMG, NatWest Markets, ING Barings, ABN AMRO and BZW are more likely to look across the Atlantic as their first priority.
